---
title: "supervised learning overview"
---

## the idea

- learn a mapping from features $x$ to known targets $y$, then predict outcomes for new observations.
- regression predicts numeric values; classification predicts categories or class probabilities.
- success means useful performance on unseen data, rather than simply fitting the training examples.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| task | target | example |
|---|---|---|
| regression | a numeric value | next-year healthcare spending |
| classification | a category | disease subtype |

:::

## model families

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| family | core idea | useful starting point / consideration |
|---|---|---|
| linear models | weighted combinations of features; ridge and lasso add penalties | fast, interpretable baselines; limited without suitable feature transformations |
| trees & ensembles | split feature space into regions; forests average randomised trees, while boosting adds sequential corrections | flexible models for tabular data; tune complexity to control overfitting |
| support vector machines | find a margin-based decision boundary; kernels allow nonlinear relationships | useful for some small or medium high-dimensional datasets; scaling and kernel choice matter |
| k-nearest neighbours | predict from nearby training observations | simple baseline; sensitive to scaling, dimensionality, and prediction-time cost |
| naive bayes | combine class probabilities with conditional feature-independence assumptions | efficient for suitable text or count data; probability estimates may need calibration |
| neural networks | learn layered nonlinear representations | useful for complex inputs such as images and sequences; architecture, data, and compute matter |
| gaussian processes | place a distribution over functions using a kernel | predictive uncertainty under model assumptions; standard methods can be costly as sample size grows |

:::

## a practical workflow

- define the target, prediction time, and metric before choosing a model.
- split data to reflect deployment: keep repeated observations from the same person together and respect time order when needed.
- fit [feature engineering](../training-evaluation/feature-engineering.qmd) within training folds to avoid leakage.
- establish a simple baseline, compare candidates with cross-validation, and tune hyperparameters on training/validation data.
- evaluate the chosen pipeline once on an untouched test set; inspect errors, calibration when relevant, and performance across important groups.

## choosing a starting point

- there is no universally best model; compare against a baseline using the same splits and metrics.
- match the loss and evaluation metric to the task and class balance.
- use the [bias–variance notes](../training-evaluation/bias-variance.qmd) to think about underfitting and overfitting.
- explore [linear regression](linear-regression.qmd), [logistic regression](logistic-regression.qmd), or [trees & ensembles](../trees-ensembles/index.qmd) next; individual topic pages are being filled in.
